notes: The Cardassian Prisoner. One of Shepard's relics rather than one of
her logs -- she collects family histories and this is the best one
she found.
**The name is held to the last two lines.** He never says it, the
interviewer never says it, and the reveal is an archival slate. The
story has to work without it, and it does: a man does eleven years in
a labour camp, walks two hundred and six people out, and refuses to
steal on the way. The name only tells a Star Trek audience *which*
man, and what it cost him to be the copy.
The arithmetic, because somebody will check it. Thomas Riker shares
William Riker's birth year, 2335; he is duplicated at Nervala IV in
2361 and sentenced to a Cardassian labour camp in 2371, aged 36.
Eight years to the solo chance he threw away (44), three more to the
escape (47), two to clear Cardassian space (49) -- and he settles on
Risa at 49, straight off the border, which is where the tape is
recorded. No gap to explain: he stops the moment he is allowed to.
Shepard is watching a fifty-one-year-old recording.
Risa is the point of the ending and not a throwaway: the most
frivolous planet in the Federation, named by a man who spent eleven
years underground and was offered anywhere in it. He says he is
settling, out loud, because that is the thing the story is for.
title: The Cardassian Prisoner
subtitle: Risan oral history project, tape eleven
author: subject interviewed at home; no surname given
extra: Fifty-one years old. One line about him in any archive.

lines.text: RISAN ORAL HISTORY PROJECT: TAPE ELEVEN
SUBJECT INTERVIEWED AT HOME. NO SURNAME GIVEN.
This is the one. This is why I keep the rack.
An old man in a garden. Not in uniform.
They gave me life. That is the sentence. Life, and a number.
Lazon Two. A mining camp. You will not have heard of it.
I was thirty-six. I thought that was the end of the story.
THE FIRST EIGHT YEARS
You learn the guard rota. Then the ventilation. Then rock.
It took me eight years to find a way out of that place.
A gap in the third shift, room for one man. I had it.
He stops and looks at something off camera for a while.
And then I did the arithmetic on who would be left behind.
Two hundred and six. I knew all their names by then.
Eight years in there. You learn everybody's name.
So I put the plan in a hole in the wall and started again.
THE NEXT THREE
Three more years to build one that everybody walked out of.
Where clever did not work, I did worse things.
Some of what I did in those three years stays off the tape.
A guard drowned in six inches of slurry. I am not sorry.
THE NIGHT
There was a shuttle on the pad outside our quarters.
A warp drive will not engage on the ground. It will try.
Everything inside a hundred metres goes inward first.
Then outward. There is very little left to count after.
They counted what they expected. Two hundred and seven dead.
He says the number like a joke he has told before.
We were four kilometres out, in the dark, holding hands.
Through the paths I found three years before and never used.
THE TWO YEARS AFTER
Getting out of Cardassian space took longer than the camp.
Freight holds. Back roads. Other people's barns. Two years.
We starved twice. Both times there was a till I could take.
Somebody asked me why I did not. I gave a poor answer then.
The real answer is I had been somebody once. I wanted him back.
Two hundred and six people came out of there with me.
Not one of them had to steal to do it. Not one.
AND NOW
At the border they asked where I wanted to be taken.
You may name anywhere in the Federation. I named Risa.
He gestures at the garden. It is a very ordinary garden.
I am forty-nine. I grow things. Nobody here knows any of it.
They have a word here for rest. I did not have one before.
I am not going anywhere else. I am settling here. Risa.
You asked would I do it again. Yes. Every day of it.
END OF INTERVIEW
SUBJECT: RIKER, THOMAS. SETTLED, RISA. NO SERVICE RECORD.
No record. He was the copy, so the file went to the other one.
Every archive I can reach gives him one line. You just read it.
